source.title: Practical Efficiency of Muon for Pretraining
source.authors: Ishaan Shah; Anthony M. Polloreno; Karl Stratos; Philip Monk; Adarsh Chaluvaraju; Andrew Hojel; Andrew Ma; Anil Thomas; A. Tanwer; Darsh J. Shah; Khoi Nguyen; Kurt Smith; Michael Callahan; Michael Pust; Mohit Parmar; Peter Rushton; Platon Mazarakis; Ritvik Kapila; Saurabh Srivastava; Somanshu Singla; T. Romanski; Yash Vanjani; A. record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It fits a parameter-dependent loss curve across model widths, but uses training loss on new batches as a proxy rather than held-out pretraining loss and does not reproduce the original studies' full scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper says it uses training loss on a new batch as a proxy for generalization error, rather than a separate held-out dataset. It reports a power-law fit to minimum loss across model sizes at fixed token count; it does not test loss scaling with tokens or compute, small-run loss extrapolation, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architecture effects on loss at fixed parameter count, downstream performance, or fit-choice sensitivity. Its optimizer and batch-size comparisons concern related loss efficiency, not any listed version.
record.test_reason: Its main aim is optimizer comparison, but in its muP/Muon width sweep (0.07B–3.67B, tokens fixed) it fits a Chinchilla-style shifted power law to minimum loss versus parameter count and compares the exponent with Hoffmann et al. That result bears directly on V1 (parameter axis only).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors' main conclusions are that Muon expands AdamW's compute-time frontier and stays data-efficient at large batch sizes, and that muP transfers hyperparameters under Muon up to 3.7B, aided by a telescoping sweep. As a side observation they report minimum loss fitting a shifted power law in parameters (exponent 0.31), which they call close to Chinchilla's 0.34.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a Gemma-based model family, a Muon/AdamW optimizer comparison, fixed-token parameter scaling, and training loss rather than reproducing the original scaling-law measurement of held-out pretraining loss across parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports variation in token efficiency with batch size, target loss, data distribution, model size, and optimizer; the final scaling fit holds tokens and the data mix fixed.

fits_no_version.finding: Muon expands the compute-time Pareto frontier over AdamW at 500M, across loss thresholds and data sets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Muon reaches target pretraining loss with a better devices-versus-time tradeoff than AdamW.

fits_no_version.finding: Muon needs 10–15% fewer tokens than AdamW for the same loss. The advantage is constant or growing with batch size, and the absolute extra tokens are roughly independent of model size (1B–4B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Muon's data-efficiency advantage over AdamW persists at large batch sizes and across model sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: The best 1B Muon run has lower training loss than the best AdamW run at every step, 0.02 nats at 2.5× the Chinchilla budget.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Muon gives lower training loss than AdamW at equal steps in the tested setting.

record.code_released: https://huggingface.co/EssentialAI (experimental artifacts stated to be released there)
record.problems: The scaling result uses training loss on new batches as a proxy for generalization rather than a separate held-out dataset. The parameter sweep is limited to 0.07B–3.67B with tokens held fixed, and the paper reports no uncertainty estimate for the power-law fit.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified values were extracted from the figure-only curves for each batch size and target-loss threshold; the paper's textual aggregate descriptions of these comparisons are recorded in R3, R4, and R6.

untested.parts: Scaling with tokens or compute. Parameter scaling beyond ~0.07B–3.7B (under two orders of magnitude). Settings other than fixed tokens, muP and Muon.
All; no small-to-large prediction is made.
All; width is varied at fixed depth, but this is not a shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
All; no variation of fitting or setup choices (the single exponent 0.31 against 0.34 is not a sensitivity test).

record.verdict_notes: The record's limits_scope label on V1 is dropped: it rested on untested parts (tokens, compute, a wider range), which belong under untested. The 'training loss rather than held-out' caveat is weaker than the record implies, since the loss is on fresh single-epoch batches. The fit has only five points, reports no uncertainty, and its points are grid minima, so R² ≈ 1 is modest evidence. The study is not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: Tests parameter-count scaling only, across a limited size range, at fixed tokens and using training loss as a generalization proxy. Does not test token- or compute-dependent power laws or held-out loss.
No test of whether power laws fitted on small runs predict losses of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for loss-minimizing parameter and token allocations.
The architecture ablation concerns token-optimal batch size, not loss changes from depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No test of power-law loss scaling beyond text/code pretraining or under repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes.
Does not systematically vary fitting choices or setups to test whether exponents or compute-optimal splits change.

rows.subject: Transformer model family aimed at approximately 3.7B parameters
rows.size_stated: 0.07B, 0.20B, 0.67B, 2.40B, and 3.67B parameter sizes are listed for the family
rows.operation_detail: Fit a shifted power law to minimum training loss across model sizes.

conditions.value: held constant across all scales; largest model trained on 160B tokens
50/50 mix of DCLM-derived web data and Stackv2-derived Python code
34 layers; sequence length 8192; batch size approximately 8 million tokens
Chinchilla-style loss fit against parameter count

rows.measure: Minimum training loss as a function of parameter count
rows.value: Shifted power-law fit: R² ≈ 1; parameter-dependence exponent 0.31; fit constant E = 1.31
rows.note: The authors describe the agreement as excellent. The tested parameter range is 0.07B–3.67B, and tokens are held constant; the measure is training loss, not a separate held-out loss.
rows.check: State should be observed, not partial. The fit is described as R² ≈ 1, with exponent 0.31 against Chinchilla's 0.34. The narrow range (~52×, about 1.7 orders of magnitude) and the fixed tokens are untested parts, not a weaker effect. The measure is training loss on unseen batches with no epoching, which the authors argue matches held-out loss. The fit uses only five sizes and three free parameters, and each point is the minimum over a hyperparameter grid. Locator should be Section 3.4 and the Figure 14 caption (Appendix H).

rows.subject: 3.7B model in the transformer model family
rows.operation_detail: Report the final training loss at the selected weight decay and muP base learning rate.

conditions.value: 50/50 mix of DCLM-derived web data and Stackv2-derived Python code

rows.value: 1.61 nats; described as outperforming all models at previous widths
rows.note: The result gives one model's loss and a qualitative comparison, not enough by itself to establish the power-law form.
rows.check: This is a single model's final loss, and it is already one of the points in R1's fit. On its own it says nothing about the power-law form, so it should not be linked to V1.

rows.subject: 500M-parameter Gemma-based models
rows.operation_detail: Compare compute resources and elapsed time required to reach target losses across batch sizes for AdamW and Muon.

conditions.value: multiple thresholds, including 1.3, 1.5, 1.8, 2.0, and 2.4 nats on Python, and 3.1, 3.15, 3.25, 3.75, and 4.0 nats on DCLM

rows.measure: Compute-time Pareto frontier for reaching target training loss
rows.value: Muon expands the Pareto frontier; the text says the expansion is consistent across tested thresholds and data distributions
rows.note: This compares optimizer efficiency, not a power-law relation between loss and parameters, tokens, or compute.

rows.subject: 1B, 2B, and 4B Gemma 3 models

conditions.value: 3.2 nats for the stated cross-size comparison

rows.value: For a target loss of 3.2 nats, all three model sizes need around 2B extra tokens with AdamW than with Muon
rows.note: The paper describes this extra-token quantity as surprisingly agnostic to model size; it is not a test of a power-law loss fit.

rows.subject: 1B model on DCLM

conditions.value: difference reported at 2.5× the Chinchilla-optimal budget

rows.measure: Training loss difference between optimizer runs
rows.value: Muon is reported to remain lower in training loss; the difference is 0.02 nats at 2.5× the Chinchilla-optimal budget
rows.note: The paper also says Muon obtains a target loss faster in wall time. This result concerns optimizer comparison, not any listed scaling-law version.
